messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Raymond Okafor was a 55-year-old African American man who came to treatment several months after his wife died suddenly, leaving him with a PCL-5 score of 67 and a life that, in his words, no longer felt like his own. The death had been unexpected and traumatic: one evening she had collapsed at home, and by the time the ambulance arrived there was nothing anyone could do. Raymond could still picture the blur of that night in pieces — the hallway light, the stretcher, the flashing emergency lights outside the house — but just as often he was hit by the raw feeling of it without a clear picture at all, a surge of panic and grief that seemed to rise out of nowhere. From the start, ambulance sirens, talk of other people losing loved ones, and even the sight of the workplace where he painted houses were enough to pull him back toward that night. A passing ambulance on the street could make his chest tighten and his thoughts race to his wife; a conversation at work about someone’s mother or brother dying could leave him staring blankly at a wall, overwhelmed by the same grief he felt when he first heard she was gone. Each of those cues did more than upset him: they instantly felt like danger, as if something terrible were about to happen again. The siren on a city street or the sound of a service vehicle arriving at a job site could put him on edge before he had time to think, and the scene at work itself — the noise, the trucks, the talk of emergencies — became a place where threat seemed to follow him in. He noticed that remembering the event was rarely a calm recollection. The memories came as vivid images — his wife on the floor, the paramedics kneeling beside her, the look on the faces of neighbors gathered outside — and once those images surfaced, he felt emotionally flooded and then immediately on guard, as if danger were still unfolding in front of him. When those pictures broke through, they did not stay in the past; they pulled him straight back into the room, with the hallway light, the stretcher, and the flashing lights feeling close enough to touch. Afterward, even ordinary sounds and sights around him seemed to carry the same charge, as if the memory had trained him to see warnings everywhere.

Over time Raymond came to believe that the trauma had not simply taken his wife but had taken something essential from him as well. He said he did not know himself anymore and felt set apart from other people, especially when coworkers joked about family or spoke casually about the future. Once he had settled on that meaning, almost anything could confirm it: a passing ambulance, a question about someone being sick, or even hearing a neighbor mention a funeral would land as proof that the world was unsafe and that he was permanently changed by it. Those appraisals made him feel as though danger was already in the air around him, before anything had actually happened. That sense that his life had been destroyed sat heavily with him and made ordinary moments feel contaminated by loss. It also sharpened his vigilance. At night, when the house was quiet and his wife’s absence was most obvious, he found it harder to feel safe than during the day; he lay awake listening for sounds from outside, body tense and ready to react, and even inside his own home he felt on guard. He noticed that the more he told himself he was broken and isolated, the more his body stayed braced for danger, as if his mind were warning him that something terrible could happen again at any moment. Those beliefs fed back into the memories too. Having decided that he was damaged beyond repair, he walked through his days already expecting threat, so new cues stood out sharply and caught hold of him. That same conviction also kept pulling him back to the night his wife died, making the images return with a force that seemed to prove his fear about himself. When he tried to think about his wife, the pictures came quickly, but they were often followed by a blank, unbearable emotional wave that confirmed for him that the loss had shattered him. In those moments he would be flooded with the conviction that his life had been ruined beyond repair. Each time the memory returned, it left him feeling as if the danger were still present, not over and done with, and that immediate sense of threat made the pictures harder to shake. The same intrusion also led him straight back to the thought that he was broken by it and would never be the same man he had been before.

Raymond also began to manage his distress by avoiding the places and topics that set it off, though the relief never lasted. He started taking different routes to avoid ambulances whenever possible and found himself pulling away from conversations at work that turned to illness, funerals, or other people’s bereavements. The more he had come to see the world as dangerous and himself as unable to cope, the more even small things started to register as warnings — an ambulance heard two blocks away, a remark about a hospital, a neighbor’s car with the lights still on late at night. Those cues kept him scanning, and the scanning made it feel as though threat was always just beneath the surface. At his painting job, which should have kept him busy, he became uneasy around the rhythm of the workplace itself — the noise of engines, the sight of service vehicles pulling up near a site, even the mention of a colleague being late because of an emergency. Each of these moments could spark the same chain: the trigger would bring back the images or the emotional force of his wife’s death, the memories would make him feel exposed and unsafe, and the feeling of being changed and alone would push him to keep his distance from people and places that might remind him of what happened. He gradually spent less time chatting with coworkers and more time working in silence, which only deepened the sense that he was apart from others.

By the time he sought help, Raymond was sleeping poorly, checking the doors at night, and feeling constantly keyed up in a way that made him exhausted and irritable. He described moving through his days with the sense that the world could break open without warning, and that anything connected to ambulances, his work, or stories of loss could drag him back into the most painful parts of that night. Even when he was trying to keep busy, the persistent sense of danger kept the memory close, so a siren heard from inside the house or a vehicle pulling up outside his painting job could bring the whole scene back in a flash. Once that happened, the old fear returned with it, making the cue feel even more powerful and harder for him to dismiss the next time. What brought him in was the fear that he was becoming unreachable even to himself, and what he most hoped for was some way to feel safe in his own home again without being ambushed by the pictures, the grief, and the certainty that his life had ended when his wife died.
